headline: Broad 2025 budget law extends and adds tax cuts, changes SNAP, Medicaid, and student loans, boosts defense and border funding, and raises debt limit.
what_it_does: This large budget law makes the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent and adds new tax breaks, including for tips, overtime, car loan interest, and people 65 and older. It adds work requirements and other limits to SNAP and Medicaid, ends many clean-energy tax credits, and changes federal student loan limits and repayment plans. It adds tens of billions of dollars for the military, border security, and immigration enforcement, creates new immigration fees, and raises the federal debt limit by $5 trillion.

who_it_affects.how: Current tax rates and the larger standard deduction become permanent, and the child tax credit rises to $2,200 per child with a work-eligible Social Security number required.

who_it_affects.group: Workers who earn tips or overtime
who_it_affects.how: From 2025 through 2028 they can deduct up to $25,000 in tips and up to $12,500 ($25,000 for couples) in overtime pay, with limits for higher incomes.
They can take an extra tax deduction of up to $6,000 from 2025 through 2028, subject to income limits.
The cap on deducting state and local taxes rises from $10,000 to $40,000 for 2025, grows slightly through 2029, then returns to $10,000 in 2030, with lower caps for incomes over $500,000.
Their children can get a one-time $1,000 federal deposit into a new savings account for minors called a Trump account.
Work requirements expand to adults up to age 65 and parents of children 14 and older, some prior exemptions for veterans and homeless people end, and certain benefit calculations are tightened.

Starting in FY2027 and FY2028, states must pay a larger share of SNAP administrative costs and, depending on their error rates, part of SNAP benefits, and they face new limits on Medicaid provider taxes.
Starting by early 2027 most must show 80 hours a month of work, school, or community service, have eligibility checked every six months, and, from FY2029, pay some copays if above the poverty line.

who_it_affects.group: Certain lawfully present immigrants, such as refugees and asylees
who_it_affects.how: Many lose eligibility for SNAP, Medicaid, Medicare, and health insurance tax credits, and face new or higher fees for asylum, parole, work permits, and immigration court filings.

who_it_affects.group: People who buy health insurance on their own through an exchange
who_it_affects.how: They face stricter income and eligibility checks starting in 2028 and may have to repay the full amount of any excess premium tax credit they received.

who_it_affects.group: Buyers of electric vehicles and home energy upgrades
who_it_affects.how: Tax credits for new and used clean vehicles end after September 30, 2025, and credits for home energy improvements and home solar end after 2025.

who_it_affects.group: College students and student loan borrowers
who_it_affects.how: Starting July 1, 2026, Grad PLUS loans end, new borrowing caps apply, and new loans are limited to a standard plan or a new income-based Repayment Assistance Plan, while SAVE, PAYE, and ICR borrowers must switch plans by July 2028.
Crop price supports, crop insurance subsidies, payment limits, and disaster aid increase, and farm programs are extended through 2031.
Full first-year write-offs for equipment and domestic research costs become permanent, and several business and international tax rules change.
The Defense Department gets about $150 billion in added funding, including money for housing, health care, tuition aid, and child care for service members.

who_it_affects.group: People who send cash money transfers abroad
who_it_affects.how: A new 1% tax applies to transfers paid with cash, money orders, or similar paper payments.

who_it_affects.group: People exposed to radiation from nuclear testing or uranium mining
who_it_affects.how: The federal compensation program is restarted, payments increase, and more areas and workers become eligible.

when_it_takes_effect: Signed July 4, 2025; provisions phase in on different dates, mostly from 2025 through 2028, with some changes as late as 2030 or later.
